causal-factors.name: Ongoing early-2026 death pace
causal-factors.rationale: 606 deaths by end of February 2026; if March–April match or exceed this pace, 1,000+ by May becomes plausible.

causal-factors.name: Historical base-rate context (annual Mediterranean deaths ~2,1xx–2,5xx)
causal-factors.rationale: Past years regularly record 2,000–2,500 Mediterranean deaths, so reaching 1,000 by May is within established base rates.

causal-factors.name: Spring crossing conditions and seasonality
causal-factors.rationale: Spring typically sees more crossings as seas calm and temperatures rise, increasing total deaths risk.

causal-factors.name: Search-and-rescue capacity and policy environment
causal-factors.rationale: Potential constraints or reductions in SAR could raise fatalities, lifting the chance of crossing 1,000 by May.

causal-factors.name: Data verification lag and undercount risk
causal-factors.rationale: IOM updates counts over time; late verifications could push cumulative totals above 1,000.

causal-factors.name: Pace of Mediterranean deaths in early 2026 (through February)
causal-factors.rationale: Approximately 606 deaths had been recorded by late February 2026, implying that if March–April maintain a similar pace, the 1,000-death threshold by end-April becomes plausible. (Sources: Guardian Feb 23, 2026; AP/UN reports cited in multiple outlets.)

causal-factors.name: Historical base-rate for Mediterranean deaths (2,000–3,000 per year range in recent years)
causal-factors.rationale: Recent years show annual Mediterranean deaths around 2,100–2,500, and 2023–2024 data support a high baseline that makes reaching 1,000 by April feasible if conditions persist. (Sources: Guardian Feb 23, 2026; DW/AP summaries of 2023–2024 figures.)

causal-factors.name: Weather and storm activity increasing crossing risk (e.g., Cyclone Harry in January)
causal-factors.rationale: Early-2026 reporting attributes higher fatalities to dangerous seas and storms, which elevate mortality risk on crossings. (Sources: Le Monde Feb 12, 2026; related reporting.)

causal-factors.name: Data completeness and missing-person reporting uncertainty
causal-factors.rationale: The Missing Migrants Project also records many missing cases that are not always verifiable, introducing ambiguity about the true toll and its trajectory. (Sources: Guardian Feb 23, 2026; UN briefings.)

causal-factors.name: Policy/SAR changes and tougher migration controls potentially reducing crossings
causal-factors.rationale: Growing migration controls and enhanced search-and-rescue coordination could deter crossings or reduce fatalities, though evidence on net effect is mixed. (Sources: Guardian coverage of EU/Italy policy and SAR debates; UN Geneva briefing context.)

causal-factors.name: Current pace through March–April 2026
causal-factors.rationale: As of late February 2026 (~606 deaths), continuing at a similar pace into March–April could push the total past 1,000 by end-April.

causal-factors.name: Weather/sea conditions in the Central Mediterranean
causal-factors.rationale: Adverse seas and storms raise mortality risk for crossings, potentially increasing the March–April death toll.

causal-factors.name: Search-and-rescue capacity and policy environment
causal-factors.rationale: Increased SAR presence or safer policy environments could reduce fatalities by improving rescue outcomes.

causal-factors.name: Origin-country push factors and sustained crossing incentives
causal-factors.rationale: Ongoing conflicts and economic hardship may sustain high demand to cross the Mediterranean.

causal-factors.name: IOM data reporting and potential revisions
causal-factors.rationale: If early-year counts are revised downward, the probability of reaching 1,000 by May would be dampened.

synthesis: Reaching 1,000 Mediterranean migrant deaths by end-April 2026 remains plausible but is exposed to downside risks from March–April pace, SAR/policy changes, and data revisions. Calibrating downward from the 0.91 ensemble, a probability around 0.75 with a 0.65–0.85 range reflects these uncertainties while acknowledging the underlying high early-2026 pace.
